summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. The province of Sivas stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in Sivas is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That national framework includes a draft legislative threat at the level of penalty. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, with participation in same-sex marriage ceremonies or celebrations carrying up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and repeated evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers of such care for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected.

The baseline recorded for Türkiye is that homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and that trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from Turkish military service. A health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Anyone subject to conscription or its documentation carries that record forward.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible; the outcome of the 11th Judicial Package as of the sources' reporting is separate and unresolved.

Enforcement climate is set by national-level decisions that provincial authorities in Sivas apply as elsewhere. Amnesty International's Report 2025/26 records that in June 2025 the authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans Pride marches in Istanbul, that police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and that over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.

Two further national indicators bear on expectations. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'. Türkiye placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.
tangentialFactors:
Blanket bans combined with case-by-case prosecutions under Law No. 2911 form the enforcement climate applying to provincial authorities in Sivas as across Turkey, so a visitor should expect national practice rather than local discretion to govern demonstrations, marches and any public visibility.

The ILGA-Europe 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking places Türkiye 47th of 49 countries, a comparative position consistent with the enforcement record documented by Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch.

Early-2026 press reports of contemplated legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' indicate continuing legislative turbulence alongside the 11th Judicial Package, and the removal of anti-LGBTQ provisions from the 12th judicial reform package shows that outcomes of individual bills have varied.

The dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025 signals that association and organising carry litigation risk, which extends to participation in any event a visitor joins.

Legal gender change has been available in Türkiye since 1988 and requires sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission, a procedure residents of Sivas use the same national courts to pursue.

There is no comprehensive Turkish law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no statutory discrimination claim to bring in employment, services or housing on those grounds.

Openly LGBTQ conscripts are disqualified from military service under a health regulation classifying homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness'; conscripts who declare it must supply photographic evidence, and the resulting 'unfit report' can circulate and affect later public-sector and private employment.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and the 2026 passage of the 12th judicial reform package without its anti-LGBTQ provisions left only symbolic same-sex ceremonies possible.

Resident LGBTI association organisers face dissolution orders of the kind issued against the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025, and 92 people prosecuted nationally for pride march participation remained on trial at the end of 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No local Sivas statute, police practice, health facility or documented incident involving trans visitors appears in the assembled sources; the province-level picture is unresolved rather than confirmed as clear, and the national framework described here is what the sources do support.

The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is not resolved beyond the 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch report: whether it was introduced, amended or dropped is not sourced here.

The relationship between the 11th Judicial Package and the 12th judicial reform package that passed in 2026 is not sourced, and the current status of the early-2026 reports on criminalising public advocacy is likewise not confirmed.

Whether Sivas provincial authorities apply the Law No. 2911 ban-and-prosecution pattern observed in Istanbul and İzmir is not documented in these sources.
